title: The Sin You Keep Calling a Struggle May Have Become Something You’ve Decided to Protect
paragraphs: The Sin You Keep Calling a Struggle May Have Become Something You’ve Decided to Protect
There is a terrifying difference between falling while you are fighting sin… and quietly arranging your life so the sin you say you hate never has to die.
There is a question most of us would rather never be asked.
Not because we do not know the answer.
Because somewhere underneath the worship songs, the Bible verses, the church attendance, the Christian posts, the promises to God, and the repeated prayers for freedom…
we may already know.
What if the sin you keep calling your “struggle” is no longer merely something you are struggling against?
What if, somewhere along the way, you started protecting it?
Read that slowly.
Because there is a difference between a wounded Christian crawling away from temptation and a Christian secretly leaving the door unlocked so temptation can come back tonight.
There is a difference between falling into a pit and furnishing it.
There is a difference between being ambushed and keeping the enemy’s phone number.
There is a difference between saying, “God, please deliver me,” while removing access to sin…
and saying, “God, please deliver me,” while carefully preserving every pathway that takes you back to it.
And perhaps that is why Paul’s words in Romans 13 are so painfully direct.
He does not speak as though darkness is something Christians should negotiate with.
He writes:
“The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near.”
Then comes the response:
“ἀποβαλώμεθα οὖν τὰ ἔργα τοῦ σκότους…”
Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness.
Not rename them.
Not domesticate them.
Not explain them until they stop frightening us.
Cast them off.
And then Paul reaches the devastating conclusion of Romans 13:14:
“ἀλλὰ ἐνδύσασθε τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, καὶ τῆς σαρκὸς πρόνοιαν μὴ ποιεῖσθε εἰς ἐπιθυμίας.”
Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh with respect to its desires.
That word deserves our attention.
“πρόνοιαν” — pronoian.
Provision.
Forethought.
Planning ahead.
Paul is not merely confronting the sinful act after it happens.
He reaches backward into the architecture surrounding the sin.
The planning.
The access.
The environment.
The little arrangements that make tomorrow night’s failure easier.
In other words, Scripture does not merely ask, “Did you sin?”
It forces us to confront another question:
“What have you been arranging so that this sin can survive?”
That question hurts.
Because sometimes what we call weakness is accompanied by preparation.
You deleted the conversation…
but memorized the number.
You confessed the pornography…
but kept the private browser, hidden account, unfiltered device, and late-night isolation that continually lead you back.
You said the relationship was pulling you away from Christ…
but kept enough emotional access to reopen it whenever loneliness became stronger than conviction.
You told God you were finished with the gossip…
but still sit eagerly in conversations where another person’s reputation becomes entertainment.
You asked Jesus to heal your bitterness…
while replaying the offense every night because anger has begun to feel strangely comforting.
You prayed for freedom from envy…
then continued feeding yourself an endless stream of other people’s lives until gratitude became almost impossible.
You asked God to free you from sexual immorality…
but kept flirting with the very boundary you begged Him to strengthen.
You said you wanted sobriety…
but preserved the relationships, locations, routines, or secret supply that made relapse conveniently available.
Different sins.
Same frightening possibility.
We can ask God to kill what we keep feeding.
And then wonder why it refuses to die.
Please understand something important before shame twists this message into something Scripture does not say.
The existence of temptation does not mean you are fake.
Being tempted is not the same thing as consenting to sin.
A Christian can genuinely hate a sin and still fall terribly.
A Christian can relapse.
A Christian can stumble repeatedly.
A Christian can cry after doing the very thing he promised God he would never do again.
The Bible is brutally realistic about human weakness.
Peter denied Jesus after insisting he would die for Him.
David committed horrifying sins.
The disciples repeatedly misunderstood Christ.
And Paul himself describes the agonizing conflict with sin in Romans 7.
Christian maturity is not sinless perfection.
Our hope has never been that we become morally impressive enough for God to tolerate us.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
But grace must never be twisted into permission to preserve what crucified our Savior.
The frightening question is not simply whether you have fallen.
The question is what you do with the road that led you there.
Do you barricade it?
Or maintain it?
Do you expose the secret?
Or improve the hiding place?
Do you remove the opportunity?
Or merely promise yourself you will be stronger next time?
Do you confess because you want forgiveness while secretly hoping nothing actually has to change?
There is a difference between someone who falls while fleeing temptation…
and someone who continually redesigns life so temptation remains comfortably accessible.
Jesus Himself spoke with shocking seriousness about dealing radically with sin.
In Matthew 5, when speaking about lust, He used the severe imagery of tearing out an eye and cutting off a hand rather than allowing sin to rule us.
Christ was not commanding bodily mutilation.
A removed eye cannot cure a sinful heart.
His language exposes something far deeper:
Do not treat casually what is destroying you.
That is why repentance sometimes looks painfully practical.
Block the number.
Delete the account.
Move the computer.
Stop going there.
Tell somebody.
Confess what secrecy has protected.
Put accountability where privacy became dangerous.
Leave the relationship that continually requires disobedience to sustain it.
Stop calling “discernment” what is actually gossip.
Stop calling lust “just looking.”
Stop calling emotional adultery “just friendship.”
Stop calling unforgiveness “having boundaries” when what you are actually preserving is hatred.
Stop calling greed “ambition.”
Stop calling pride “knowing your worth.”
Stop calling compromise “being human” when you have already decided you will not surrender it.
Not every boundary will look identical for every person.
But repentance eventually becomes visible.
Because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel guilty enough to behave better.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
For the exposed.
For the person reading this with a secret nobody knows.
For the believer who has prayed the same embarrassed prayer at 2:13 in the morning more times than they can count.
For the person who whispers,
“Jesus… I did it again.”
There is something you need to know.
Christ already knows the room you keep locked.
He knows the search history.
He knows the messages.
He knows what happened on the trip.
He knows the money.
He knows the addiction.
He knows what you watched.
He knows who you touched.
He knows who you hate.
He knows the fantasy you replay.
He knows what happened when everyone thought you were asleep.
He knows the version of you nobody at church has ever met.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is enormous.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He went because sin brings guilt, corruption, slavery, separation, and death.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore judgment for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith finds something human effort could never purchase:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new standing before God.
A new heart.
A new Master.
A new direction.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past can be forgiven.”
Grace also teaches us that our old master no longer owns us.
That is why Romans 13 does not end with “try harder.”
Paul says:
“ἐνδύσασθε τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.”
Put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the center.
Christ.
Not behavior modification without Christ.
Not shame.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Jesus Christ.
You do not defeat darkness merely by staring harder at darkness.
You come into the light.
You put on Christ.
You fill the spaces previously designed for sin with the things of God.
Prayer where there was secrecy.
Scripture where there was fantasy.
Fellowship where there was isolation.
Confession where there was hiding.
Worship where there was self-indulgence.
Accountability where there was convenient privacy.
Obedience where there was negotiation.
And when you fall?
Run toward Jesus, not away from Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Return.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not because sin does not matter.
Precisely because Christ does.
First John 1:9 gives believers extraordinary hope: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Notice the Gospel beauty of that.
The answer to hidden sin is not better hiding.
It is coming into the light.
Maybe that is what God is confronting in you right now.
Not merely the sin.
The provision.
The backup plan.
The doorway.
The relationship.
The password.
The bottle.
The app.
The private conversation.
The resentment.
The convenient excuse.
The environment you know makes obedience nearly impossible.
Maybe you have spent months praying:
“Lord, take this away.”
And perhaps tonight another prayer needs to follow:
“Lord, show me what I have been protecting.”
That prayer can become expensive.
Because God may put His finger on something you desperately want to keep.
And suddenly you understand why you kept calling it a struggle.
Calling it a struggle allowed you to mourn it without necessarily surrendering it.
But repentance eventually reaches the keys.
The passwords.
The schedule.
The relationships.
The money.
The habits.
The private room.
The places nobody else can see.
Because Jesus does not merely want the Sunday version of you.
He is Lord over Monday night too.
He is Lord over your phone.
Your body.
Your sexuality.
Your thoughts.
Your finances.
Your anger.
Your relationships.
Your loneliness.
Your browser history.
Your ambitions.
Your wounds.
Your secret life.
Everything.
And surrender may feel like death because, in a very real biblical sense, something is dying.
The old way.
The protected darkness.
The fantasy of belonging to Christ while keeping one private throne for yourself.
But what waits beyond surrender is not emptiness.
It is freedom.
Maybe imperfect freedom at first.
Maybe trembling freedom.
Maybe freedom that still requires accountability, counseling, discipleship, boundaries, tears, difficult conversations, and daily dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
But freedom nonetheless.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
If Scripture is exposing something in you right now, do not waste the moment defending yourself.
Run to Christ.
There is no need to impress the One who already knows everything.
Tell Him the truth.
Maybe your prayer tonight is embarrassingly simple:
“Jesus, I don't just want forgiveness for touching this again. I want to stop protecting the road that keeps taking me back.”
That may be where the war changes.
Not when temptation disappears.
But when you stop helping it find you.
And when you see someone else saying those words, do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
There are battles people cannot safely explain in a Facebook comment.
Let the Church remember how to carry wounded people toward Jesus instead of turning confession into spectacle.
Not because these words are magical.
Do not make provision for the flesh.
And there may be someone in your life who keeps begging God for freedom while unknowingly—or perhaps knowingly—preserving access to the very thing enslaving them.
Send this privately if that would protect their dignity.
Someone scrolling quietly tonight may be losing a battle nobody knows exists.
Your share may place a biblical warning—and the hope of Jesus Christ—in front of someone who would never admit they went searching for it.

If Gospel Warrior has helped point you toward Christ, consider following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Stay close for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot donate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot merchandise your way into righteousness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
The call is to repent and believe the Gospel.
So tonight, before another promise…
before another apology…
before another deleted history…
before another tearful “God, this is the last time”…
look around.
What are you still protecting?
What door have you deliberately left unlocked?
What provision have you made for the flesh while praying for the Spirit to give you victory over it?
Bring it into the light.
Destroy the provision.
Run to Jesus.
Because perhaps the greatest evidence that you truly want freedom is not that you never stumble again.
It is that you stop building comfortable places for your chains to live.
And if you fell yesterday, hear the Gospel one more time:
your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Peter's denial did not write his final chapter.
The shame of sinners does not intimidate Christ.
The cross still speaks.
The tomb is still empty.
Grace still calls sinners out of darkness.
Jesus still receives the repentant.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
And Jesus is still worthy of whatever you have been afraid to surrender.
So bring Him the secret.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the version you can explain away.
The real one.
Because the thing you drag into Christ's light no longer has to control you from the darkness.
You keep asking Jesus to break the chain. Tonight, ask Him to show you whether your own hands are still protecting the key.
